GeometryConstructionsFractions
Game: See how two circles can cut a segment into exactly equal pieces, however you drag its ends.
How to play: Drag the dots A and B, press + or − to choose how many pieces, and tick Show hint to reveal the triangles behind the trick.
N = 3
Look for the math

There is a way to cut a segment into N equal pieces without measuring any of them. Draw two circles, join the places where they cross, and the chord marks off exactly one N-th. Move the ends of the segment and it keeps working. Nathan Besteman found the construction; it appeared in Mathematics Teacher in 2005. Bogomolny's applet lets you drag it.

Setting up the circles

Start with the segment AB and its midpoint M. Put C on the same straight line so that AC = N·AM = N·AB/2. Now draw a circle centred at A through B, and another centred at C through A. Their radii are AB and AC, and they meet at D and E. The small grey dots along AC mark the half-steps AM, 2·AM, …, N·AM.

The chord stands straight up

Both D and E are the same distance from A as from C, so the line DE is the perpendicular bisector of AC: it meets AC at right angles. Call that meeting point P. The right triangles APD and ACQ share the angle at A, so they are similar triangles. Here Q is the midpoint of DA, just as the applet draws it.

Two lines of the proof

Similar triangles give the page's first equation, AP/AQ = AD/AC. But AQ = AD/2 by construction, and AD = AB because both are radii of the circle centred at A. Substituting gives the page's second equation:

AP = AB²/(2 AC)

Nothing here depends on how long AB is or where the segment sits on the page — only on the ratio between the two radii.

Choosing C finishes the trick

Because C was placed so that AC = N·AB/2, the formula collapses to the page's final claim:

AP = AB/N

So the green dots at AP, 2·AP, …, N·AP really are the N equal fractions of AB. The logic test checks all three equations, the perpendicular chord and the equal spacing for every N from 2 to 20 and hundreds of placements of A and B, and compares the whole picture with a second transcription of the applet's own circle-intersection code. The claim holds in every case.

Try dragging B close to A and setting N to 20: the marked-off piece shrinks to one twentieth, yet all twenty dots stay evenly spaced.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
